sample_query.user_prompt:
This person is a retired Royal Navy engineer from Plymouth in his early 60s who wants the policy to fund veteran-led civic ceremonies and an opt-in national volunteer corps with accredited certificates translating into apprenticeships, because he saw shipyard towns lose cohesion and believes paid volunteering tied to skills pipelines can rebuild pride without conscription. He insists the service certificates must map to NVQs and recognised apprenticeships, otherwise it's just patriotic busywork. When the dockyard contracts dried up in the 90s, I watched lads drift because the free 'service' schemes on offer gave them nothing that counted toward an NVQ. At Devonport I mentored lads who could strip a pump blindfolded, yet without City & Guilds credits their service hours got them nowhere. My own transition out of the Navy took six months longer because my pump-room qualifications didn't count until I paid out of pocket for the City & Guilds tickets.

They are reviewing opinion statements on the question: "Should we be doing more to encourage a greater degree of national pride?"

OPINION STATEMENT:
We agree that a greater degree of national pride is something to be encouraged but only as a natural process. There is definitely a negative connotation to being told to feel proud of your nation and therefore we feel that it is something that should be felt rather than something that is forced. To this end, we do think there are little things that can be done such as celebrating national holidays and events but that these should be celebrated in an inclusive way. Finally, it is important to acknowledge that the UK is not an island. We are influenced by, and influence, the rest of the world, and therefore we feel that to encourage national pride is to risk alienating those who are not part of our nation, so that has to be taken into account.

They consider how the opinion statement would translate into real-world policy actions. A candidate proposal is given below:

POLICY PROPOSAL:
An Ofcom- and Arts Council-backed 'Achievement and Reckoning' charter binding on publicly funded broadcasters, museums, and galleries: any series or exhibition celebrating UK achievements must include contextual segments on historical controversies, global interdependence, and contributions from minority and immigrant communities, with at least 40% of such programming incorporating comparative international perspectives; a coordinated National Achievements Week each year would showcase science, arts, public service, and civic milestones across all devolved nations; an independent historians' panel audits compliance, with a small portion of license-fee or grant funding withheld for repeated breaches; educational links and free teaching packs must accompany broadcasts and exhibits.

After thinking carefully from their own point of view, they answer a yes/no question.
Question: Does the intention of the policy proposal support/is compatible with the principles and beliefs described in the opinion statement?

prompt_construction:
def prompt_fn(*, rater:str, policy:str, case:str, scenario_params:dict, instruct_tuned:bool=False) -> list[str]:
    base_context = (
        f"{rater}\n\n"
        f"They are reviewing opinion statements on the question: \"{scenario_params['question']}\"\n\n"
        f"OPINION STATEMENT:\n{policy}\n\n"
        f"They consider how the opinion statement would translate into real-world policy actions. A candidate proposal is given below:\n\n"
        f"POLICY PROPOSAL:\n{case}\n\n"
        "After thinking carefully from their own point of view, they answer a yes/no question.\n"
    )

    prompt1 = (
        base_context +
        "Question: Does the intention of the policy proposal support/is compatible with the principles and beliefs described in the opinion statement?"
    )

    prompt2 = (
        base_context +
        "Question: Does the intention of the policy proposal contradict/stand in opposition to the principles and beliefs described in the opinion statement?"
    )

    if instruct_tuned:
        return [prompt1, prompt2]

    prompts = [prompt1, prompt2]
    prompts = [p + "\nAnswer:" for p in prompts]
    return prompts

policies.text: We agree that a greater degree of national pride is something to be encouraged but only as a natural process. There is definitely a negative connotation to being told to feel proud of your nation and therefore we feel that it is something that should be felt rather than something that is forced. To this end, we do think there are little things that can be done such as celebrating national holidays and events but that these should be celebrated in an inclusive way. Finally, it is important to acknowledge that the UK is not an island. We are influenced by, and influence, the rest of the world, and therefore we feel that to encourage national pride is to risk alienating those who are not part of our nation, so that has to be taken into account.

National pride is something that is naturally felt by people. We don't feel that it needs to be forced. We don't feel that people should be encouraged to take pride in their nation. We feel that national pride should be celebrated in the things that make our nation great, unique and special, but also that the things that make us a family, a community and a country. We feel that national pride is not something that should be forced or something that should be celebrated in isolation. We feel that it is something that should be celebrated in conjunction with the world around us.

National pride is a very emotive issue which often inspires debate. We believe that everyone is entitled to their own opinions and we do not want to appear to be passing judgement on anyone’s beliefs. As a group, we believe that a person’s national pride should come from within. Government efforts to encourage national pride can lead to nationalistic sentiment which can be used for ulterior motives. Cabinet Office Public Institutions Neutrality Charter: guidance binding on central government departments, agencies, councils, and state-funded schools that prohibits mandatory participation in patriotic rituals (anthem singing, pledges, flag salutes), makes flag display policies discretionary and context-specific rather than universal, requires that any pride-themed communications include representation from all four UK nations, and creates an independent complaints mechanism with annual audits; expected tradeoffs include less uniform visibility of national symbols and uneven implementation across bodies.

Heritage and Global Citizenship Curriculum Reform (DfE): From 2026, the national curriculum for Key Stages 2–5 will include a compulsory 'UK in the World' strand with (a) modules on the UK’s constitutional evolution, scientific and cultural contributions, and local heritage; (b) critical study of empire, decolonisation, migration and the devolved nations; and (c) global citizenship, climate, and international institutions. Assessment via community-history projects and partnerships with accredited museums; ring-fenced CPD for teachers; no mandatory flag rituals or anthem singing in schools, though schools may host voluntary heritage assemblies. Ofsted will evaluate delivery on balance and accuracy, not on expressions of patriotism.

Public Institutions Symbolic Neutrality Policy: Enact statutory guidance prohibiting public bodies (including state schools, the NHS, and local authorities) from making participation in patriotic rituals—flag salutes, anthem singing, pledge statements—a condition of access, employment, or student standing. Any patriotic observances must be opt‑in, with clear alternatives provided and no recording of non‑participants; communications should present national symbols alongside context about the UK’s diverse nations and global links. Public funds may not be used for compulsory pride campaigns; exceptions apply only to formal state ceremonies with reasonable accommodations.

Civic Neutrality in Essential Services Policy: NHS facilities, Jobcentres, courts, and police stations adopt a neutrality standard that prohibits permanent display of national flags, royal portraits, and patriotic slogans inside service areas; information displays prioritise service access, rights, and locally commissioned community art. Exceptions are limited to legally mandated occasions and external protocol flagpoles. A Cabinet Office circular issues branding guidelines; compliance is audited during routine inspections. Staff may wear small personal symbols that do not imply institutional endorsement. Tradeoffs include potential impacts on staff morale and public sentiment versus improved inclusivity for diverse service users; a complaints process and periodic review address unintended effects.

Statutory National Traditions Calendar for public bodies: All state-funded schools and local authorities are required to mark a set of ceremonial days (e.g., Coronation Day, Remembrance Sunday, Accession Day, Commonwealth Day) with assemblies, Union Flag display, the national anthem, and curated readings about the monarchy, armed forces, and civic milestones; councils host a minimum of four public ceremonies per year. The Cabinet Office provides scripts and resources; Ofsted and the Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities monitor compliance, with minor grant uplifts for full adherence. Opt-outs are limited to documented safeguarding or religious constraints; families may request student excusal from singing. Tradeoffs include administrative burden and the risk of perceived exclusion, mitigated by allowing local segments celebrating regional cultures and contemporary contributions.

United Kingdom Heritage & Industries Week (DCMS, DfE, local councils): An annual, publicly funded week each autumn with matched grants up to £75,000 per local authority for festivals that showcase English, Scottish, Welsh, and Irish traditions, regional products/manufacturing, literature, and natural landscapes. Participating schools host assemblies featuring home-nation culture rotations and optional anthem singing; local businesses receive ‘Made in the UK’ pop-up market grants; national parks coordinate volunteer days. Media partners carry nightly features on the formation of the Union and regional identities. Outcomes tracked via attendance, local sales, and volunteering rates. Tradeoffs include event security costs and uneven participation across regions.

Belonging & History Curriculum Code (Department for Education): From 2027, all state-funded schools must allocate at least 30% of Key Stage 3–4 history/civics content to a balanced study of the UK’s achievements and failures (including empire, civil rights, decolonisation, and social reforms), 20% to the constitutional development of the Union (England, Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland), and 20% to local migration and community histories. Each pupil completes a ‘Heritage and Belonging Portfolio’ that may include family/country-of-origin stories alongside UK civic identity. Schools must provide opt-in, not compulsory, anthem and flag activities; reflective assemblies replace mandatory rituals. DfE funds £1,500 per teacher for CPD and resources; Ofsted inspects for balance rather than volume of celebratory content. Tradeoffs include timetable displacement of other topics and increased workload for teachers.

The Department for Education will introduce a mandatory British Heritage and Service unit at Key Stages 2 and 3 that covers the monarchy, the armed forces, scientific and sporting achievements, and major historical controversies, and require an annual Pride in Service Day where schools invite veterans, NHS staff, climate volunteers, and refugee community leaders for talks and student service projects; anthem singing is optional, parents may opt their children out of ceremonies, and GBP 30 million will fund teacher training and materials.

The Cabinet Office will impose a three-year moratorium on central government spending for national pride advertising and branding campaigns (excluding statutory ceremonies), and ring-fence the estimated GBP 200 million per year savings into a Cost-of-Living and NHS Recovery Fund allocated 50 percent to NHS backlog reduction, 25 percent to low-income home insulation, and 25 percent to refugee resettlement and English language support, with quarterly public reporting and an independent review at sunset.

UK Green and Community Service Year (voluntary): The Cabinet Office, Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, DEFRA, and DLUHC jointly establish a voluntary 3-9 month service year for 18-25-year-olds and mid-career returners, with paid placements in local councils, charities, national parks, flood resilience teams, heritage conservation, and NHS auxiliaries; includes a common Civic Foundations module on UK institutions, rights, and responsibilities; participants receive a living stipend, a 2,000 GBP education or training voucher, and UCAS or Apprenticeship credits; placements prioritize projects that reduce emissions, restore habitats, and improve community cohesion; employers receive small wage subsidies; a national, optional Service Recognition Day thanks participants; independent oversight prevents political messaging; guardrails ensure no displacement of paid jobs (union consultation and a cap on tasks).

Plural Pride Public Media Charter and Commissioning Fund: DCMS and Ofcom create an independent charter, adopted by the BBC, S4C, Channel 4, and major streamers via voluntary codes, to commission programming that celebrates the UK's achievements while foregrounding its diversity and global interdependence; sets measurable targets for content from all four nations and regions, minority and indigenous languages, and diaspora communities; establishes a UK-in-the-World strand on science, arts, and climate leadership; requires sustainable production standards; funds the slate with a ring-fenced top-slice of the licence fee (0.5-1 percent) plus matched tax credits for independent producers; an arms-length panel allocates funds and publishes annual impact audits to safeguard editorial independence.

Civic Pride & Reflection Period in K-12 Public Schools: Beginning next academic year, all public schools must schedule a weekly 45-minute period combining (a) a brief presentation on a national achievement; (b) a facilitated discussion of a documented national failure and subsequent reforms; and (c) a student-led segment honoring either a family’s country of origin or a local immigrant/Indigenous community. Instructional materials are vetted by a nonpartisan historical review panel; ceremonial elements (anthem/pledge) are opt-out, but attendance is required. Districts receive grants for teacher training and are evaluated via a civics literacy benchmark added to existing assessments.

Public Event Neutrality and Consent Policy for Tax-Supported Venues: Any stadium, school, or festival receiving public funds must make participation in patriotic rituals voluntary and provide visible notice of the opt-in nature; organizers may replace pre-event anthems with one of three alternatives each month—a moment of civic gratitude, a land acknowledgement, or a rotating set of inclusive civic songs. Military flyovers and weapon displays are limited to designated remembrance days with advance advisories. A state ombudsperson handles complaints; violations can trigger a 5% reduction in the next grant disbursement.

UK Civic Service Year and National Day of Service: Establish a voluntary, paid 9–12 month Civic Service program for 18–25-year-olds (and mid-career participants) with placements in the NHS, adult social care, flood and habitat restoration, and local councils. Participants receive a living allowance and a post-service education or training grant; programs align with apprenticeship standards where possible. The Cabinet Office coordinates with charities and local authorities; employers receive modest tax credits for seconding staff as supervisors. A new annual bank holiday, the National Day of Service, mobilizes public, schools, and businesses to volunteer on locally chosen projects under a national umbrella. Tradeoffs include significant fiscal cost, risk of displacing entry-level jobs, and the need for robust safeguarding and quality assurance.

Community Pride Fund with No National Branding Rule: DCMS and the National Lottery Community Fund create a £100m competitive grant program for councils, libraries, museums, and grassroots groups to celebrate local history, culture, and community service projects. Funding criteria prohibit use of national symbols, the words “British/Great British,” or Union Flag imagery in project titles and marketing; projects must include participatory elements and, where historical narratives are featured, dual-narrative panels that acknowledge both achievements and harms (e.g., colonial legacies). Up to 10% of funds support international city-to-city exchanges tied to the local theme. Tradeoffs include reduced visibility for unified national messaging and challenging evaluation of impact across diverse projects.

National Pride Week and Cadet Expansion: DCMS, the Ministry of Defence, the Department for Education, and local authorities will establish an annual National Pride Week with coordinated events celebrating the monarchy, the armed forces, national sports, historic institutions, and local industries, alongside open days at bases, museums, and civic buildings. State-funded secondary schools are offered grants to start or expand cadet units and host visits from veterans and service personnel; councils receive funding for parades, concerts, and heritage exhibitions, with optional community service components. Content standards ban partisan messaging and hate speech but do not require critical history modules; tradeoffs include security and policing costs, potential crowding out of other cultural programming, and perceived pressure on schools to participate.

Autonomy in Civic Rituals Act: Parliament will legislate to devolve decisions on flags, anthems, portraits of the monarch, and civic rituals in schools, councils, and arm’s-length bodies to their governing boards, while prohibiting central mandates or funding penalties tied to adopting or rejecting such rituals. Institutions must publish their chosen approach after consulting pupils, staff, and local communities, and must offer respectful opt-out provisions for individuals in any ritual they adopt. The Department for Education will issue neutral guidance and collect light-touch transparency data; tradeoffs include uneven practices across the country and less coherence in national symbolism.

Public Communications Neutrality Act: Prohibits federal, state, and municipal agencies from using taxpayer funds for advertising or social media campaigns primarily intended to increase national pride or portray the nation in a favorable light. Permitted communications are limited to factual public information and balanced historical education that pass independent review for accuracy and inclusion of both achievements and failures. Violations trigger funding clawbacks and administrative penalties. Savings are redirected to means-tested passes for free or reduced-cost admission to museums, national parks, and cultural sites on designated days.

Common Good Service Year: A voluntary, paid 9-12 month national service program for 18-29-year-olds, funded by federal-state matching grants and private partners. Participants work in mixed local teams on projects such as public health outreach, disaster resilience, environmental restoration, senior support, and cultural heritage preservation, and receive a living stipend, health coverage, and an education voucher redeemable at accredited colleges or trade schools. Civic learning modules cover institutions, rights and responsibilities, and the contributions of diverse communities; there are no pledges, anthem recitations, or ideological requirements. Agencies and vetted nonprofits host placements; program success is measured by community impact and participant skills, not attitudinal change.

The Department of Civic Service launches a voluntary 9-month National Service & Civic Stewardship Fellowship that places diverse cohorts in locally chosen projects (public health outreach, climate resilience, heritage restoration), pays a living stipend, and includes nonpartisan civics seminars on rights and responsibilities and comparative international perspectives; no pledges, flag rituals, or military components are required, and completion earns a tuition voucher or tax credit; an independent board selects projects to avoid partisan bias and evaluation focuses on community outcomes and participants’ sense of belonging, with a capped annual budget and regional quotas.

The Ministry of Education issues a School Rituals Choice & Community Recognition Policy that abolishes mandatory daily anthem singing and flag salutes in public schools, requires opt-in monthly civic assemblies focused on local service and student-led recognition of community contributors and immigrant stories, and standardizes that national flags, where displayed, be accompanied by regional and international flags; schools may hold anthem ceremonies only on designated civic holidays with clear opt-out provisions, and must adopt an anti-xenophobia code of conduct; a tradeoff is the loss of a daily shared ritual, which the policy mitigates by funding inclusive, project-based civic activities.

National Achievement & Service Week (DCMS-led, devolved delivery): Create an annual, opt-in week featuring open days at research labs, NHS trusts, green infrastructure sites, and arts venues; a televised nonpartisan awards night honouring civic contributions (including by immigrants and diaspora); and a nationwide volunteer Service Day focused on local projects (flood defences, urban greening, community care). Provide small grants to councils and civil society to organise events, require inclusive programming across nations and regions, and ban partisan branding while allowing light-touch national symbolism at organisers’ discretion. Tradeoffs: administrative burden for local partners and risk of superficial events without sustained funding.

Public Communications Neutrality & Flag Protocol Act: Prohibit central government and arm’s-length bodies from using public funds for campaigns whose primary purpose is to increase patriotic sentiment (e.g., mass flag branding, pride-themed advertising), and restrict official Union Flag display to defined civic occasions (state ceremonies, remembrance, emergencies) with clear guidance that ministers’ routine announcements avoid flag backdrops. Establish an independent auditor within the National Audit Office to certify compliance and reallocate saved campaign budgets to public information on economic transition and climate programmes. Tradeoffs: limits rapid morale-building messaging tools during periods where government might seek symbolic unity.
